title: Reversible change detectives
subtitle: Separate melting, freezing and dissolving
objective: Describe melting, freezing and dissolving and explain how the starting substances can be recovered in these examples.

sow.alignment: Intentional revisit and extension of earlier solubility work; separating dissolving from melting adds depth. Original secondary-age exemplar at an upper-KS2 conceptual level; no qualification approval or completion claim.

priorLearning: Know that dissolved substances may no longer be visible.
success: Distinguish a change of state from mixing with a solvent.
Explain that dissolved sugar remains present.
Choose a suitable reverse process and state what is recovered.

vocabulary.meaning: A substance changing from solid to liquid.
A substance changing from liquid to solid.
A substance mixing through a solvent to form a solution.
A mixture in which the dissolved substance is distributed through a solvent.
Able to be changed back in the stated example or conditions.
Liquid changing to gas at its surface.

equipment: Constructed evidence cards, selected route, pencils; optional particle tokens.
preparation: The default lesson is paper-based. Keep melting and dissolving verbs separate.
Explain that particle circles are symbols, not visible grains or a to-scale molecular diagram.
safety: No heating, tasting, sealed-container warming or freezing practical is needed.
Any later practical requires separate preparation; do not heat sugar to recover it in this lesson.
practicalAlternative: Use supplied observations and particle tokens to compare processes without heat, food handling or a time-dependent trial.

misconceptions.claim: Dissolving is the same as melting.
misconceptions.correction: Melting changes one substance from solid to liquid; dissolving forms a mixture with a solvent.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a second substance is involved.

misconceptions.claim: Clear sugar solution contains no sugar.
misconceptions.correction: Sugar molecules remain mixed among water molecules even when crystals are not visible.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the recovery record shows.

misconceptions.claim: Cooling a solution always gives back all its original separate substances.
misconceptions.correction: The useful reverse process depends on the mixture and target; removing water can recover dissolved solid in this example.
misconceptions.check: Ask which substance must be removed or collected.

access.supported: Classify three cases and use a particle word bank.
access.standard: Explain process differences and use mass/recovery evidence.
access.stretch: Evaluate a disappearing-sugar claim and distinguish recovery of one component from both.
access.regulation: Offer private writing, pointing, drawing or adult scribing. Allow pass-and-return for public questions and desk-based participation. Choose support from current learning evidence, not fixed ability labels.

sources.title: American Chemical Society: Why does water dissolve sugar?
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Sugar molecules separate from one another and mix among water molecules without the sucrose molecules being destroyed.

slides.title: The crystal has disappeared from view
body: Did the substance vanish, melt or dissolve?
A detective needs more than appearance.
slides.notes: Present the question with paper evidence. No tasting is allowed or needed to identify a dissolved substance.

slides.title: State or mixture?
body: R1. Name a solid and a liquid.
R2. Does invisible always mean absent?
R3. What unit records mass?
slides.notes: Accurate examples; no; grams or kilograms. Do not assume all clear liquids are pure water.

slides.title: I identify a change of state
body: Ice and liquid water are the same substance.
Melting changes solid to liquid.
Freezing changes liquid to solid.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I track water before and after. A second substance is not required for the melting step. Energy transfer matters; warming does not need to continue raising temperature during the phase change. Numerical phase temperatures are not needed.

visual.title: Melting and freezing of water
visual.description: Two macroscopic states of the same substance are connected by opposite arrows: warming can melt ice into liquid water; cooling enough can freeze water into ice. This diagram does not represent exact density or crystal structure.

slides.title: I count what the model retains
body: Sugar molecules spread among water molecules.
The sugar symbols remain present.
A solution forms; the sugar has not melted here.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Model the four orange symbols before and after: same number, new distribution. Blue and orange symbol sizes are schematic. Sucrose molecules are not broken into atoms in this dissolving example.

visual.title: Sugar particle model
visual.description: Eight water symbols and four sugar symbols are retained in both panels. Sugar begins clustered and ends dispersed among water; no symbols disappear. Sizes, shapes and quantities are schematic.

elements.text: Dissolving: sugar remains in the mixture

Blue: water molecules. Orange: sugar molecules.
Symbols and quantities are not to scale.

slides.title: I choose a route back
body: Letting water evaporate can leave sugar behind.
Simple open evaporation does not collect the water.
Reversible does not mean instant or effortless.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Explain that the recovery observation spans days and is constructed. No rapid or heated sugar recovery is instructed. This lesson distinguishes concepts; next lesson chooses specific recovery methods.

visual.title: Recovering the dissolved solid
visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Sugar solution; Water evaporates
over time; Sugar remains
after drying. This recovers the sugar. Water is not collected
by simple open evaporation; no heating is required here.

elements.text:
This recovers the sugar. Water is not collected
by simple open evaporation; no heating is required here.

slides.title: Process evidence tribunal
body: W1. Classify A and B: melting/freezing or dissolving.
W2. Use C and D to challenge “the sugar vanished”.
State what each piece of evidence contributes.
slides.notes: A contains melting and freezing; B dissolving. C supports no loss of mass from the sealed system; D shows sugar can be recovered. Mass alone does not identify every substance.

slides.title: Choose a reverse process
body: A tray contains melted ice. A second contains sugar solution.
Which needs enough cooling? Which needs water removed to recover sugar?
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Cooling freezes water; water evaporation can recover sugar from solution. Simply putting sugar solution in a freezer is not the same as cleanly recovering both components.

slides.title: Write a precise verdict
body: W3. Repair “Dissolving makes sugar into water”.
Use the particle model and recovery record.
slides.notes: Sugar molecules remain in a mixture with water. The result is solution, not conversion of sugar into water. Keep molecular detail age-appropriate.
slides.reveal: Sugar remains mixed through the water. Removing water can leave sugar behind.

slides.title: Sugar is stirred into room-temperature water
body: The crystals become invisible and a solution forms. What happened?
slides.notes: A is correct. B incorrectly calls dissolving a change of state; C incorrectly claims that the sugar vanishes.

options.text: The sugar dissolved and remains in the solution.
options.feedback: The particles are distributed through the solvent.

options.text: The sugar melted into pure liquid sugar.
options.feedback: This is mixing with water to form a solution, not melting.
The mass and recovery evidence contradict disappearance of the substance.

slides.title: Your independent investigation
body: Choose one response route.
Compare melting, freezing and dissolving.
Explain a route to recover the stated substance.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across the three You do slides. Supply shared page 1 and one selected route page. All routes target the stated science objective; a labelled drawing or independent dictated explanation is valid.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Track the substance before and after.
Use mass and recovery evidence appropriately.
Name what a chosen process actually collects.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask pupils which evidence supports their explanation. Read prompts or scribe without supplying the scientific conclusion.

slides.title: Check before sharing
body: Does my explanation answer the question?
Have I named the evidence or process?
Have I kept the conclusion within its limits?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Use the route-specific worked answers to identify one precise next step.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Share one corrected process label.
Check the before-and-after substance.
Improve a disappearing or melting claim.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Offer partner or private teacher feedback. Ask for one specific revision linked to evidence; no public ranking.

slides.title: A question worth investigating
body: Suggest one next question about this lesson’s evidence.
Choose a question whose answer would improve our model.
slides.notes: Lundy cycle: invite written, spoken or pointed suggestions. Select one feasible question and explain how the pupil contribution changes the next example or investigation.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: E1. How is melting different from dissolving?
E2. Where is the sugar in a clear solution?
E3. How could sugar be recovered here?
slides.notes: Melting changes the state of a substance; dissolving makes a mixture. The sugar remains distributed through the water. Evaporating the water over time can recover sugar. E4 asks for the reverse of melting: freezing.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: change detectives
pupilPages.intro: Records C and D are constructed examples. All work can be completed without a practical.

cards.title: A • Ice record
cards.text: Solid ice changes to liquid water when energy is transferred in. Later, enough cooling turns the liquid back into ice.

cards.title: B • Sugar record
cards.text: Sugar crystals are stirred into room-temperature water. The crystals are no longer visible; the liquid stays clear. No tasting is used.

cards.title: C • Mass record
cards.text: Constructed data: sealed container and contents are 120 g before dissolving and 120 g after. Nothing is added or removed while dissolving.

cards.title: D • Recovery record
cards.text: Constructed observation over several days: water leaves an open sugar solution by evaporation; dry sugar remains. No class trial or heating took place.

cards.title: E • Distinction
cards.text: Melting is a solid-to-liquid state change. Dissolving mixes a substance through a solvent; a clear solution can still contain the dissolved substance.

cards.title: F • Boundary
cards.text: The diagrams model the stated physical examples. “Easy to reverse” alone is not a complete test for whether any unknown change is physical or chemical.

blocks.prompt: W1. Name the processes in A and B.
W2. What do the mass and recovery records show about sugar?
W3. Repair “Dissolving makes sugar into water”.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: choose the process
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Word bank: melting / freezing / dissolving / solution.

blocks.prompt: S1. Ice becomes liquid water. This is …
S2. Liquid water becomes ice. This is …
S3. Sugar mixes through water. This is …
S4. Explain where the sugar is after crystals are no longer visible.
S5. Choose how to recover sugar: remove water by evaporation / pretend it vanished. Explain.
S6. Does open evaporation collect the water as well?

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: process report
pupilPages.intro: Track the starting substance and the result.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the table with the lesson examples.
N2. Explain the difference between melting and dissolving.
N3. Use both C and D to challenge “the sugar no longer exists”.
N4. Describe how to recover sugar and state which component open evaporation does not collect.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: evidence and recovery
pupilPages.intro: Explain the limits as well as the useful result.

blocks.prompt: T1. Compare melting ice and dissolving sugar using substances, states and particle arrangements.
T2. Does a constant mass of 120 g alone prove exactly what substances are present? Explain why recovery evidence adds information.
T3. Evaluate “Cooling any mixture always returns all starting materials separately”. Use the two cases.
T4. Explain why recovering sugar by open evaporation is different from recovering both sugar and water.
E1. How is melting different from dissolving?
E2. Where is the sugar in a clear sugar solution?
E3. How can sugar be recovered in this example?
E4. What process reverses melting of water?
Reflection. Which change would need a different recovery method?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: Valid solid/liquid examples; invisible does not mean absent; grams or kilograms.

answers.label: W1–W3 / reverse routes
answers.answer: A melting and freezing; B dissolving. C shows unchanged total mass in a closed system; D shows recoverable sugar after water leaves. Enough cooling refreezes melted ice; evaporation removes water to recover sugar. W3 sugar remains distributed in a mixture with water, not converted into water.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A correct. B confuses dissolving with melting. C incorrectly claims the substance ceases to exist.

answers.label: S1–S6
answers.answer: Melting; freezing; dissolving; sugar remains mixed through the water; evaporation removes water leaving sugar; no, simple open evaporation does not collect water.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: Melting: ice→liquid water; freezing: liquid water→ice; dissolving: sugar plus water→sugar solution. N2 state change versus mixture formation with solvent. N3 same total mass plus sugar recovery contradict sugar vanishing; neither observation requires tasting. N4 allow water to evaporate over time; sugar remains, water is not captured by open evaporation.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 water remains water while state/arrangement changes; sugar and water remain present as a mixture, sugar molecules distributed among water molecules. T2 constant mass indicates no measured mass loss from the system but does not identify all substances; recovery specifically supports sugar remaining. T3 cooling refreezes water but does not universally separate every mixture into original components. T4 open evaporation leaves solid while water vapour escapes; recovering water requires capturing vapour and condensing it, explored next lesson.

answers.label: E1–E4 / assessment
answers.answer: State change versus mixing; sugar remains distributed; evaporate water; freezing. Secure: distinguishes processes and gives an appropriate recovery route with its target. Re-teach by drawing one water substance versus two components in a solution. Reflection accepts a relevant alternative target.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.
This is an intentional deeper revisit of earlier solubility work: the new focus separates dissolving from state change and distinguishes recovery of one component from both.
All particle pictures are selective models, with unchanged symbol counts but no claim of exact molecular size or concentration. Sugar dissolving is chosen so whole sucrose molecules remain intact.
Paper evidence reproduces every interactive decision. Evaporation over days is a constructed record, not a process claimed to finish during the 40-minute lesson.

interactive.title: Change tribunal: track the substance
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
